newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Security Council approves force for E. Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Security Council approves force for E. Zaire.

text.p: As hundreds of thousands of refugees trekked home to Rwanda, the U.N. Security Council on Friday authorised an international force to bring food and medicine to those still stranded in eastern Zaire.

In a resolution adopted unanimously, the 15-member body approved deployment of a multinational force until March 31 to bring aid to the refugees, despite Rwanda's claims it was no longer necessary because the refugees were returning.
But Canada's ambassador Richard Fowler told the council and reporters afterwards that the exodus of the refugees did not exclude the need for a large number of troops.

"Despite the heartening news that up to a third of the Rwandese reguees in Zaire may finally be going home, people will continue to die in eastern Zaire in appalling numbers and their presence there will continue to destablize the region," he said.
"Close to a million refugees will remain at risk, even if the reports of current refugee flows into Gisenyi (Rwanda) are fully accurate," he added.
Canada will lead the force after which the United Nations will organise a follow-up operation, if necessary. Fowler said more than 20 countries had offered over 10,000 soldiers.

While the council was putting the finishing touches on the document, about a third of the more than 1.2 million refugees abandoned camps in Mugunga near Goma and began to move towards the Rwandan border. Rwanda's U.N. ambassador Gideon Kayinamura said that the exodus meant the force was no longer "relevant" and the world should send aid to his country instead.
But U.N. spokeswoman Sylvana Foa said the refugees still needed aid and troops were necessary to handle the logistics.
She said about 700,000 refugees remained "in desperate need of help," adding that those in the Goma area were relatively better fed.
British Ambassador Sir John Weston said he had been told by the U.N. refugee officials that the refugees had confidence to return to start moving home because of the impending arrival of the troops.

Asked about difficulties of setting up staging areas for troops inside Rwanda, he said contacts "we have had with senior members of the Rwandan government in the last few days have been quite encouraging."
The refugees first fled to eastern Zaire in 1994, fearing reprisals from Rwanda's new Tutsi-led government after more than 500,000 Tutsis were killed by Hutu extremists.
But the armed Hutus lost control of the camps during the latest crisis, sparked by fighting between ethnic Tutsis in Zaire who are battling Rwandan Hutus and the Zairean army.

Troops expected to go in first are from Canada, the United States, Britain, France, Senegal, Italy, Spain and the Netherlands. The United States will take over the airport at Goma in eastern Zaire. All the Europeans, including British and French contingents will be further south in Bukavu, French ambassador Alain Dejammet told Reuters.

Others countries offering troops are Austria, Portugal, Sweden, Ireland, South Africa, Argentina, Brazil, Congo, Cameroon, Ethiopia, Mali, Egypt and Nigeria. Finland, Norway, Germany and Israel are expected to help with humanitarian aid.
The cost of the new multinational force would be borne by participating nations but the United Nations is setting up a fund to help African states pay for their troops.

During the debate antagonisms between Zaire and Tutsi-led Rwanda and Burundi were evident. Zaire's U.N. envoy, Lubaku Khabouji N'Zaji, implied Rwanda was allowing refugees back to cut short the time troops would be in the area.
"For two years they have been living like animals and now the Rwandese cabinet goes to the border to welcome them. The council should not allow itself to be duped," he said

The task before the international community, however, is daunting for troops, diplomats and U.N. officials, who must plan for a follow-up operation in March and monitor the refugees' movements in Rwanda, where jails are crammed with thousands of people accused in the 1994 genocide.
